title: Matthew 26:26–30
context: During the Passover meal Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper: bread as His body, the cup of the covenant in His blood poured out for many for the remission of sins. He points ahead to drinking new with them in His Father’s kingdom, then they sing a hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.)

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On the cup of the covenant in His blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Jesus took the bread - the bread or cake, which the master of the family used to divide among them, after they had eaten the passover. The custom our Lord now transferred to a nobler use. This bread is, that is, signifies or represents my body, according to the style of the sacred writers.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 26:26–30)

reformed.quote: And while they were eating, Jesus took bread. I do not understand these words to mean that with the paschal supper was mixed this new and more excellent supper, but rather that an end was then put to the former banquet. This is still more clearly expressed by Luke, when he says that, Christ gave the cup after that he had supped; for it would have been absurd that one and the same mystery should be broken off by an interval of time.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 26:26–30)

verses.text: As they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks for it, and broke it. He gave to the disciples and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives—then commands: Take, eat; this is my body. The gift is offered to disciples at the table for reception by faith.

Arminian interpreters emphasize the sincere offer in the sacrament. Christ truly presents Himself crucified for sinners; grace enables a free taking and eating in faith, not a mechanical force. The broken bread summons trust in His self-giving.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Lord’s own hands interpret the meal. Blessing, breaking, giving, and the word “this is my body” bind sign to Christ’s body given for His people.

Reformed sacramentology (without settling every intramural debate here): Christ authoritatively attaches the bread to His body. The Supper is His gift and command, received by faith as He feeds those He has claimed.

verses.text: He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave to them, saying, “All of you drink it,
verses.arminianNotes:
Thanksgiving, then a cup given with Drink of it, all of you. The invitation is corporate and earnest—every disciple addressed.

“All of you” fits a sincere gospel hospitality at the table. Grace enables each to drink in faith; none is told the cup is a fiction for some and reality for others in the outward call of the meal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Thanks and distribution come from Christ. “All of you” binds the Eleven (and the table company under His word) to one cup He interprets.

The command is Christ’s. Participation is discipleship under His lordship; the meaning of the cup follows in His next words.

verses.text: for this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.
verses.arminianNotes:
The cup is covenant blood, poured out for many for forgiveness. Jesus centers salvation in His atoning death—blood that remits sins.

Arminian readers gladly preach a sufficient atonement sincerely offered in the gospel, received by faith. “For many” magnifies the wide saving purpose of the cross without turning forgiveness into automatic possession apart from trusting Christ. The Supper seals what faith receives: sins forgiven through His blood.
verses.reformedNotes:
Covenant blood, poured out for many, for forgiveness—this is the heart of the meal. Jesus interprets His death as the covenant sacrifice that remits sins.

The “many” are the people Christ effectively redeems; the cup proclaims a definite, powerful atonement. Forgiveness is not a vague mood but blood-bought covenant mercy.
verses.keyContrast: Both adore the blood of the covenant for forgiveness. Arminians underline a sufficient atonement sincerely offered and received by faith (“many” as the wide gospel scope); Reformed Christians emphasize an effectual atonement for the many given to the Son, proclaimed and sealed in the Supper.

verses.text: But I tell you that I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father’s Kingdom.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus frames the cup with hope: a pause until the kingdom feast with them. The Supper looks back to the cross and forward to shared joy.

The promise is personal (“with you”) and inviting. Grace sustains disciples through the dark night toward a future table with Christ.
verses.reformedNotes:
Abstaining now, feasting then: eschatology saturates the cup. The Father’s kingdom will host new wine with His people.

Christ’s vow is sure. The Lord who pours out covenant blood guarantees the reunion banquet for those united to Him.

verses.text: When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
verses.arminianNotes:
They sing a hymn and then go out to the Mount of Olives. Worship does not stop when the path turns toward Gethsemane. They go out with praise still on their lips.

Grace enables praise and obedience together. Singing is a fitting response before the trial of watching and praying.
verses.reformedNotes:
Psalm-shaped praise, then the mount. The story moves under God’s script toward arrest and cross.

Word, sacrament, song, and then the appointed place. Providence leads from table to olives without dropping the thread of Christ’s purpose.
